Step by step instructions ⬇️ Supplies Needed:  Spray paint, shovel, rake, work gloves, hand tamper/plate compactor, weed barrier, paver sand, your chosen pavers (we used 24”x16”), level, plastic edging & stakes, hammer, utility knife, wheelbarrow, tape measure, white marble rock, Dominator Mulch Glue, garden sprayer, and Dominator Wet Look Paver Sealer. Here’s how ya do it: ➡️Clear and roughly level your area, ensuring a slight slope for drainage. Compact the soil thoroughly. Mark your walkway's perimeter with spray paint (ours is 48” wide!), then install plastic paver edging firmly along your lines. ➡️Lay down landscape weed barrier and secure it with stakes. Spread 1-2 inches of paver sand, smoothing it out (don't compact yet!). Start laying your pavers, maintaining consistent spacing (we used an 11-inch gap between our 24”x16” pavers, using a 24”x11” styrofoam guide). Gently tap each paver level with a rubber mallet, adding sand underneath if needed. For extra stability, we nailed two plastic edging stakes on each side of every paver. ➡️Spread your rock evenly around the pavers, (ours vary in size from 1/2”- 2”) making sure it's level with the paver tops. Rinse and wash all dust and dirt from the rocks and pavers – let them dry completely! Then, spray Dominator Mulch Glue generously over the marble rock (undiluted, up to 3 coats or larger rock) letting it dry between applications. Finish by applying two thin coats of Dominator Wet Look Paver Sealer to your pavers, backrolling any excess. We tore up our own backyard to save over $4,000 and honestly… I’d do it again. 😅 This is Part 3 of our DIY paver patio series: the budget breakdown. We were quoted $6,000+ for a patio extension, so my husband and I decided to tackle this backyard renovation ourselves. Here’s what it actually cost: • Skid steer rental for excavation: $350 • Plate compactor rental: $75 • Landscaping fabric: $60 • Truckload of leveling sand: $350 • 350 sq ft of pavers (delivered): $935 • Polymeric sand for the paver joints: $90 • Edge restraints (that I hated): $130 • Miscellaneous DIY tools + concrete blade: $100 Total DIY patio cost: $2,090. After laying the pavers, we made all the edge cuts with an angle grinder and somehow managed to get the transition to our existing patio looking pretty dang professional. I even ditched the border bricks I bought and “shopped” my own backyard for free landscaping rocks instead. 😂 This DIY backyard makeover ended up being cheaper than the poured concrete quotes we received, but I love that paver patios add so much more character, texture, and curb appeal. If you’ve been debating a DIY patio installation, consider this your sign that it might be more achievable than you think. Now we’re moving on to the DIY outdoor kitchen, so follow along for the final backyard reveal. ✨

Five plants that separate a designed garden from a planted one. Rosemary — most people treat it as a herb. Designers use it as a structural evergreen with silver foliage, late winter bloom, and serious drought tolerance once established. Echinops — steel-blue globe thistle that holds its form into winter. Pollinators love it, it seeds around just enough, and nothing else gives you that texture. White Cloud Nepeta — all the soft billowing habit of catmint, none of the blue. Cleaner in a white or silver palette. Underused because most people don’t know it exists. Mountain Hydrangea (Hydrangea serrata) — more refined than arborescens, lacecap form, better fall color, and it actually performs in part shade without flopping. Blue Mist Fothergilla (Fothergilla gardenii ‘Blue Mist’) — blue-green foliage all season, then flame in fall. Native, compact, and genuinely beautiful. The plant that makes clients ask “what is that?” #gardendesign #landscapedesign
